title: Coaching with Care
author: Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes applies findings from the 'Generative AI Can Harm Learning' research to a use case the paper did not address: AI-powered instructional coaching for teachers. Her structural move is to transfer the student finding, that over-reliance on AI produces outsourced thinking, surface engagement and false confidence, onto teachers, warning that ready-made lesson plans, scripts and strategies may erode the reflective practice professional growth depends on, while teachers perceive improvement they have not actually built. The design principle she draws from the study's GPT Tutor condition is that the tool must prompt an attempt and a reflection first, functioning as a thinking partner rather than a directive expert, which she links to Kraft, Blazar and Hogan on coaching that works by fostering agency and inquiry. She also imports the paper's 'jagged frontier' warning, noting that AI may advise well on routines or questioning and poorly on complex domains such as SEND, which is her argument for human-in-the-loop design. The piece is not anti-AI: it grants real opportunities in personalised observation feedback, on-demand strategies and scalable support where human coaches are unavailable, provided design prioritises teacher thinking rather than shortcutting it.
points: The transfer is the contribution: a finding about students outsourcing thinking to AI is applied to teachers, where the same mechanism would erode the reflective practice coaching exists to build.
The false-confidence risk is the sharp one, since teachers may perceive improvement while failing to build the underlying expertise, which makes the harm invisible to the person experiencing it.
The design rule drawn from the study is concrete: prompt an attempt and a reflection before offering anything, so the tool acts as a thinking partner rather than a directive expert.
The jagged-frontier point gives a domain-specific warning, strong AI advice on routines and questioning alongside poor guidance on SEND, which is the case for human-in-the-loop design.

The opportunities are stated fairly, personalised observation feedback and scalable support where no human coach exists, with the condition that design must prioritise teacher thinking over convenience.
quotes: The core finding from the paper is that when students over-rely on AI, they tend to outsource their thinking, leading to surface-level engagement and poorer long-term learning outcomes.
If AI provides ready-made answers (lesson plans, scripts, classroom strategies), it may erode the reflective practice that underpins professional growth.
The paradox is clear: while AI can increase short-term productivity, it risks weakening the very thinking processes that coaching is meant to develop.
AI might provide strong advice on routines or questioning techniques but poor guidance on complex domains such as SEND.

This is why if we are using AI to instructionally coach, we must design human-in-the-loop systems, to safeguard teacher judgement and ensure nuanced decisions remain with qualified teachers and coaches.
The goal must be to stimulate metacognition and strengthen professional autonomy, not replace it.
When thoughtfully designed as a co-pilot rather than an autopilot, AI can stimulate reflection, inquiry and growth, enhancing rather than undermining teacher professionalism.
